Constructive mathematics / from the ground up

Mathematics on
a finite machine.

Build the computer. Make its limits visible.
Ask what mathematics we can construct inside it.

A mathematical symbol is small. What it asks us to do may not be. To construct a value, run a program, or check a proof, we need somewhere to store the work and time to carry it out.

We begin below the notation, with a switch. From switches we build logic, memory, and a tiny computer. Then we ask how definitions and proofs should account for the computer’s limits.

Read straight through, or use the contents to jump. In bit grids, green means 1; pale means 0. Each figure labels what its colors mean.

This first part is executable. The proposed route from bounded constructions to analysis is a research direction, with its open obligations stated explicitly.

1 / A physical beginning

A switch controlled by a signal #

A MOS transistor has a gate terminal and a conducting path between source and drain. Voltage at the gate controls that path. Here we idealize it as a switch: either conducting or open.

An nMOS switch conducts for a high input; a pMOS switch conducts for a low input. Pair them between the supply and ground, and their shared output gives the opposite of the input.

Physical basis: Computation Structures, CMOS. Real voltage thresholds, capacitance, leakage, and switching delays are outside this ideal digital model.

2 / From voltage to a rule

Two values, then logic #

Definition 2.1 · Bit. A Bit has exactly two values, 0 and 1, also called low and high. Equality compares these values. The operation not exchanges them.

A NAND gate returns 0 only when both inputs are 1. In CMOS, the pull-down uses two nMOS switches in series; the pull-up uses two pMOS switches in parallel. Both inputs must be high to connect the output to ground.

Tie the inputs together and NAND becomes NOT. Invert a NAND output and we obtain AND. Invert both inputs before a NAND and we obtain OR. These identities let us assemble more complex finite logic.

not(a)    = NAND(a, a)
and(a, b) = not(NAND(a, b))
or(a, b)  = NAND(not(a), not(b))

3 / A value that persists

Remembering a bit #

A combinational gate answers its present inputs. Memory retains a value. Feedback allows a circuit to have stable states; a controlled write changes which state it holds.

One implementation uses cross-coupled gates as a latch. A clocked flip-flop can combine latches so that input is captured at a clock edge. We now abstract this circuitry as a one-bit register: on a rising edge, copy D into Q; otherwise preserve Q.

This is an ideal edge-triggered register, not a timing simulation. Physical setup and hold times and metastability require a more detailed model. Sequential logic background.

4 / State and transitions

A computer small enough to see #

Give the machine four words of data memory, each four bits wide. The accumulator A holds a working word. The two-bit program counter PC selects an instruction; the four-bit instruction register IR holds the instruction just fetched.

Definition 4.1 · Instruction. An instruction is a four-bit word. Its first two bits select HALT (00), LOAD (01), NOT (10), or STORE (11). Its last two bits select a data address for LOAD and STORE.

Each Step performs a whole instruction: fetch into IR, decode, then update state. This is a register-transfer model. A physical processor would split that work into clocked phases.

With four steps, 0101 is loaded, complemented to 1010, stored at address 01, and the program halts. Try a budget of two. The machine stops before STORE: the result is out of steps, not a failed logical claim.

5 / Making the limit part of the object

A construction can run out of room #

Finite memory alone does not guarantee termination: a machine can revisit a state and loop. A finite step budget bounds an attempt. Every larger budget is another finite allowance, not permission to finish infinitely many steps.

Design proposal 5.1 · Bounded construction. A construction consumes explicit state and resources, returning either a value with new state, a rejection, or resource exhaustion.

construct(input, state, budget)
  → ok(value, newState, remainingBudget)
  | rejected(reason)
  | exhausted(resource)

A type specifies valid representations and evidence. A constructor may try to produce an inhabitant; a checker may try to validate one. The constructor’s inability to finish does not show that the type has no inhabitants.

The allocator below is implemented. The general type-and-effect notation is a proposal, not yet a language or a verified typing calculus.

For a set-like collection we must additionally define equality, membership, and duplicate handling. For a stateful reference we must specify which snapshot it describes. A changing container and a mathematical set are different objects; one does not define the other automatically.

6 / What counts as evidence?

A proof has a domain #

Proposition 6.1. For every b : Bit, not(not(b)) = b.

Proof. If b is 0, the two operations give 0 → 1 → 0. If b is 1, they give 1 → 0 → 1. These are all the values of Bit. Each branch reduces to equality of identical values. □

The existing kernel checks this finite case split. Its internal constructor names are low and high. The checker runs as a separate browser module; compiling it to instructions of our small computer remains future work.

Not checked
Proof evidence
No checker result yet.

State is useful. It is not a consistency theorem.

The barber specification asks for a person who shaves exactly those people who do not shave themselves. Applying that rule to the barber requires P ↔ not P. No Boolean value satisfies it. Changing state over time can describe alternation, but that is a different specification from the original simultaneous condition.

We can avoid admitting this object by restricting formation rules. To justify such restrictions, we still need a precise language, semantics, and a soundness argument.

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems concern sufficiently expressive, effectively axiomatized arithmetic theories under consistency assumptions. Finite hardware does not invalidate them. A fixed finite domain can be exhaustively checked in principle; an extensible theory reasoning about arbitrary computations may again meet the hypotheses. A bounded proof search that stops without a proof settles neither truth nor provability.

Gödel’s original paper. Our current finite checker makes no claim to decide all arithmetic or to prove its own consistency.

The project’s question is therefore precise: which claims can a declared machine construct and check, with which resources, and under which rules?

7 / Toward analysis

Numbers beyond a single word #

A four-bit word encodes integers from 0 through 15. We can define exact addition when the sum fits and return overflow otherwise. Wrapping modulo 16 would be a different operation.

Proposition 7.1. Checked four-bit addition is commutative as a result: exchanging the inputs preserves either the exact value or the overflow outcome.

Not checked

This exhaustive check proves a finite statement. It does not yet provide addition on arbitrarily large integers. Multiword arithmetic would need allocation rules and its own correctness argument.

Floating point is an approximation with algebraic costs

Floating point stores a finite significand and exponent. Rounding makes arithmetic practical, but familiar laws need checking. With ordinary finite operands and a fixed rounding mode, addition is commutative; associativity can fail. Special values such as NaNs also complicate equality.

In this browser’s binary64 arithmetic, let a = 10¹⁶, b = −10¹⁶, c = 1.

(a + b) + c = ?
a + (b + c) = ?
Floating-point associativity. This is a host arithmetic example, not an instruction implemented by our tiny computer.

A real number as a request for precision

An alternative is a procedure that, for a requested error bound, attempts to produce a rational enclosure. A successful result includes evidence that the value lies inside. More precision can require more memory and work.

For √2, start with [1, 2]. Bisect the interval. If the midpoint squared is below 2, retain the upper half; otherwise retain the lower half. Squaring and comparison can use exact integer arithmetic.

The engine checks the enclosure inequalities after each successful refinement. If the next comparison exceeds the bit limit, the last enclosure survives. Nothing has constructed an infinite digit string.

Research direction 7.2. A computable-real representation should supply arbitrarily accurate approximations when given sufficient resources, with a specified convergence guarantee. A procedure that can fail at every finer precision does not establish such a real.

To build analysis we still need rational arithmetic with explicit bounds, compatible refinement, an error specification, and proofs that operations preserve it. General equality of computable reals is not decidable. Continuity, limits, and differentiation need constructive hypotheses and witnesses; finite experiments alone will not establish them.

On a fixed device we can execute only finitely much of this process. A theory may reason about a family of larger finite budgets. Keeping that distinction visible is the foundation we want to investigate.

Bauer & Kavkler, Implementing real numbers with RZ: a connection between specifications and computable real arithmetic. Our bounded demonstration is not their full construction.

Reading & references

How this book is taking shape #

Distill is the editorial reference: a continuous argument with figures the reader can manipulate. The mathematical references motivate compact definitions, explicit hypotheses, and careful separation of a formal theory from the structures it describes. This book develops its own text and constructions.

  1. Hohman, Conlen, Heer & Chau. Communicating with Interactive Articles. Distill, 2020.
  2. Roman Kossak & James Schmerl. The Structure of Models of Peano Arithmetic. Oxford University Press, 2006. A reference for the theory–model distinction, not a claim that a finite word machine models Peano arithmetic.
  3. Walter Rudin. Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill, 1976. A reference for the definition–theorem–proof progression toward analysis; its classical foundations are not imported without examination.
  4. Computation Structures: CMOS and Sequential Logic. Electrical and circuit background.
  5. Kurt Gödel. Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I, 1931.
  6. Oracle Numerical Computation Guide: Associative Operations.
  7. Andrej Bauer & Iztok Kavkler. Implementing real numbers with RZ, 2007.

The next construction should earn its place: define it, implement it, prove what we can, and account for the work.
